title: A canal between two oceans
text: A ship passing through the Panama Canal climbs, in effect, a flight of stairs. The channel rises eighty-five feet above the sea, and locks {{1}} the vessels up and down in giant concrete chambers — a solution nobody had originally wanted. The French, who began the project in 1880, had {{2}} on digging a sea-level passage in the style of Suez, and the mistake proved {{3}}: disease-ridden jungle and landslides killed more than 20,000 workers and {{4}} the company bankrupt. The Americans, taking over in 1904, made the decisive choice — build locks, control the rivers, and defeat the mosquitoes: Colonel Gorgas drained swamps and screened windows, cutting the death rate from yellow fever to almost nothing within two years. The canal opened in 1914, {{5}} the sea journey between New York and San Francisco by some 8,000 miles. Its economics have never stopped {{6}}: tolls are paid per container, and a single transit can cost a shipping line over a million dollars. Expansion in 2016 let the largest modern vessels through, though drought has since {{7}} the water that powers the locks. A century on, the canal remains what its builders intended: the {{8}} between two oceans, and one of the great engineering bargains of history.

gaps.explanation: 'locks lift the vessels up and down' — raise them between levels; list = tilt, limp = walk badly, loom = appear threateningly.
'had counted on digging a sea-level passage' — planned on it; court = pursue romantically or seek favour, coax = persuade gently.
'the mistake proved fatal' — deadly, with more than 20,000 killed; fateful = momentous for the future, furtive = secretive.
'left the company bankrupt' — caused it to end up bankrupt; 'led bankrupt' is ungrammatical (lead to bankruptcy).
'shortening the sea journey by 8,000 miles' — reducing its length; shepherd = guide like a shepherd, shelter = protect.
'have never stopped fascinating' — the verb 'stop' takes the gerund; 'fascinated' would mean the economics themselves were interested.
'drought has since reduced the water' — there is now less of it; reuse would be a remedy for drought, not a consequence.
'the link between two oceans' — the connection; the other nouns share the 'li-' spelling but are unrelated.
